{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Cuisine of Italy|Cuisine of Italy]] | [[Cookbook:Meat|Meat]]

'''''Ossobuco''''', when loosely translated from Italian, means hollowed bone; a reference to the large piece of marrow in the center of the veal shank bone.<ref>[http://www.answers.com/topic/osso-buco Definition of ''ossobuco'' on Answers.com]</ref> It's a Milanese speciality of veal shanks cooked in meat broth and flavored with white wine.<ref>[http://www.foodnetwork.com/recipes/giada-de-laurentiis/osso-buco-recipe/index.html Giada De Laurentiis' recipe for ''ossobuco'' on the Food Network website]</ref> Slowly braised, this relatively tough, yet flavorful cut of meat becomes meltingly tender, and the connective tissues and marrow dissolve into the sauce, making it rich and creamy. 

The shank is a relatively cheap cut of veal which is readily available in most good supermarkets and butcher shops. Look for meaty hind-shanks cut from the top of the thigh <ref>[http://visual.merriam-webster.com/food-kitchen/food/meat/cuts-veal.php Cuts of veal as displayed on Merriam-Webster.com]</ref> with a high proportion of meat to bone. Each piece should be about five inches across and one-inch to one-and-a-half inches thick.

This dish probably had its origins in a Milanese farmhouse during the late nineteenth century and most likely did not originally include tomatoes, a New World vegetable.<ref name= "Clifford A. Wright">[http://www.cliffordawright.com/caw/recipes/display/bycategory.php/recipe_id/726/id/38/ Info from Clifford A. Wright on ''ossobuco'']</ref> ''Ossobuco'' first became popular in the ''osterie'' of Milan, which were neighborhood restaurants of Italy's large cities.<ref name="Clifford A. Wright"/> These catered to the neighborhood's local residents but rarely if ever to tourists and foreigners.<ref name="Clifford A. Wright"/>

Traditional ''ossobuco'' was prepared with cinnamon, [[Cookbook:Allspice|allspice]], bay leaf and ''[[Cookbook:Gremolata|gremolata]]'' and today is called ''ossobuco in bianco'' (''ossobuco'' in white sauce). The modern version has, by and large, replaced the older one. This new version includes tomatoes and ''[[Cookbook:Mirepoix|mirepoix]]'': carrot, celery and onion, flavored with herbs but no ''gremolata'' (although hybrid versions exist which include both tomato and ''gremolata''). ''Risotto alla milanese'' is traditionally served with ''ossobuco'', but goes well with [[Cookbook:polenta|polenta]] or mashed potatoes.<ref name="Clifford A. Wright" />

== Ingredients ==
* 4 slices [[Cookbook:Veal|veal]] hind shank, about 2.5–4 centimeters (1–1½ inches) thick
* 1 medium [[Cookbook:Onion|onion]], [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]] fine
* 3 ribs [[Cookbook:Celery|celery]] with leaves, chopped fine
* 1 medium [[Cookbook:Carrot|carrot]], chopped fine
* 2 cloves [[Cookbook:Garlic|garlic]], [[Cookbook:Mincing|minced]]
* 3 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] [[Cookbook:Butter|butter]] 
* 4 tablespoons [[Cookbook:Vegetable oil|vegetable oil]]
* 240 [[Cookbook:Milliliter|ml]] (1 [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]]) dry white [[Cookbook:Wine|wine]] or white [[Cookbook:Vermouth|vermouth]]
* About 480 ml (2 cups) meat [[Cookbook:Stock|broth]]
* 3 tablespoons [[Cookbook:Tomato Paste|tomato paste]]
* 6 [[Cookbook:Anchovy|anchovy]] fillets, mashed
* ½ [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] dried [[Cookbook:Thyme|thyme]]
* 2–3 [[Cookbook:Bay Leaf|bay leaves]]
* 2 strips [[Cookbook:Lemon|lemon]] peel
* [[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]]
* Fresh ground [[Cookbook:Pepper|pepper]]
* [[Cookbook:Flour|Flour]]

== Procedure==
# Preheat [[Cookbook:Oven|oven]] to {{#invoke:Temperature|f|350}}.
# If the butcher has not done so, tie the shanks around the middle with kitchen twine; this will keep them from falling apart during cooking.
# Choose a heavy, covered roasting pan or [[Cookbook:Dutch Oven|Dutch oven]] which will just accommodate the veal shanks in one layer. Put the butter, two tablespoons of the oil, the onions, celery and carrots in the pan and [[Cookbook:sweat|sweat]] over medium heat until the vegetables have wilted—about 8 minutes. Add the garlic and lemon peel and [[Cookbook:sweat|sweat]] until they're fragrant, about 2 minutes more. Remove from the heat.
# Meanwhile, heat the remaining oil in a [[Cookbook:Skillet|skillet]] until it is near the smoking point. Lightly flour the veal shanks and slip them into the oil. Richly brown the shanks on both of the cut sides, then place them in the roasting pan on top of the vegetables.
# Place the wine in the skillet and [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]] until reduced by one-half, [[Cookbook:Deglazing|deglazing]] the bottom of the pan. Pour this over the veal shanks.
# Heat the beef broth to a boil in the skillet, whisking in the tomato paste and anchovies. Add this to the veal shanks, along with the herbs, several grindings of pepper, and a large pinch of salt. The liquid should cover three quarters of the shanks. If not, add extra water.
# Bring the pot to a [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]], cover, and place in the oven. Cook for approximately 2 hours, turning and [[Cookbook:Basting|basting]] the shanks every half hour. If you notice that the cooking liquids have nearly evaporated, add hot water, about one half cup at a time. The veal is done when it is fork tender and falling from the bone.
# Transfer the shanks to a platter, remove the strings, and cover to keep warm. If the sauce seems watery, as is probable, place the pan on the stove top over high heat and reduce the cooking liquid until the sauce has a thick, creamy consistency. Pour the sauce over the shanks and serve.

== Notes, tips, and variations ==
* There are variations to this dish that use other animal shanks including beef, turkey and [[Cookbook:venison|venison]].
* The recipe calls for anchovies, which enrich the finished sauce without adding a fishy flavor. Don't omit them, even if you don't like anchovies.
* Traditionally, the cooking sauce is finished with a mixture of garlic, lemon zest and parsley called ''gremolata.'' It adds a burst of freshness to the finished dish. ''Gremolata'' consists of the grated zest of one lemon, one finely minced clove of garlic, and one tablespoon of finely chopped parsley. Add this mixture to the sauce at the end of the cooking, as it's being reduced.
* ''Ossobuco'' is almost always served with [[Cookbook:Risotto|''risotto'']]. It's one of the few examples of Italian cooking where a starch is served with the main course. One may, for a change, substitute ''orzo'' or ''ancini de pepe'' cooked in meat broth and finished with butter and [[Cookbook:Parmesan Cheese|parmesan cheese]].
